description: We are Moonlanders, a six-person team of engineering and computer science students from Mansoura. We build web apps, handle data, and design user-friendly interfaces, with each member owning a clear part of the project.
summary: The Moonlanders helps people explore where and when a lunar mission might land. Visitors can browse sites on an interactive Moon, check seven-day forecasts for sunlight and direct Earth visibility, and enter their own lunar coordinates. A site view shows the local skyline, periods of light and contact, and possible interruptions. Visitors can compare two sites during the same week, rank the best start times for one site, or rank sites for a chosen time. The results help start planning conversations, but the current terrain and scores are illustrative and do not assess landing safety.
details:
Choosing a lunar landing site is also a question of timing. Near the Moon’s south pole, the Sun skims the horizon. A ridge can be lit while nearby ground stays dark, and Earth can disappear behind the landscape. We built The Moonlanders to help people explore those changes before they commit to a place or a date.

The website starts with a Moon visitors can turn and zoom. Pick a UTC day to see the modeled daily outlook at 18 curated locations, including polar ridges, Artemis candidate regions and historic landing sites. A seven-day forecast card for each location shows how its score changes through the week. Visitors can also enter their own lunar latitude and longitude for the same first-pass forecast.

The Moon view makes the sites easy to locate before opening a detailed forecast.

The weekly outlook shows which days change, rather than reducing a site to one number.

Opening a site brings the visitor down to the surface. The 360-degree skyline places the Sun and Earth against the modeled local horizon. Visitors can play or move through the selected week to see those positions change. The page also lays out sunlight and direct-to-Earth visibility as time windows, with the longest contact and blackout periods, daily scores, terrain context, scientific opportunities and engineering challenges. A sunny week can still contain a communications gap; we show those conditions separately.

The site view connects the forecast to a view from the ground.

When a site looks promising, visitors can test it against another. Compare holds the dates steady and places two locations side by side, including their surface skies, day-by-day changes, visibility windows and modeled constraints. Best time searches 24-hour starts within a chosen week for one site. Best site starts with a UTC time and ranks the curated locations over the following six hours. The rankings are meant to lead people back to the underlying light and Earth-contact windows, where they can see why an option moved up or down.

Compare keeps the week fixed while the location changes.

Best time ranks possible starts for one chosen place.

Best site ranks places for one chosen start time.

For early mission planning, the website offers a quick way to shortlist places and dates for deeper study. For students and the public, it makes lunar polar trade-offs visible. We connected a Moon-wide view, a surface view and two directions of search: “Where should we go at this time?” and “When should we go to this place?” Visitors can also test a point outside the curated list.

We built the website with TypeScript, React and Next.js. Three.js supports the interactive Moon and terrain visuals; Recharts presents changing values. astronomy-engine supplies the live Sun and Earth positions. We used NASA’s challenge-posted JPL Horizons for separate reference timelines, and the challenge-posted Quickmap and Moon Trek to study lunar places and how to present them. NASA LOLA elevation products informed the terrain research. No special hardware is needed to use the website.

The current live terrain is synthetic and LOLA-informed, so its terrain-blocking results and scores are illustrative. Seeing the Sun does not establish power output; seeing Earth does not establish a working radio link. The website identifies those limits next to the results and explains the sources and calculations in Method & Data. We considered that honesty essential: a helpful shortlist must not be mistaken for landing approval or a safety assessment.

Open the live website.
